abstract: |
  Temperature forecasts one to four weeks ahead support frost warnings and
  agricultural planning in the tropical Andes, where machine learning has
  rarely been tested at subseasonal leads. We present an artificial intelligence forecasting
  system for weekly mean temperature anomalies at five Peruvian stations
  between 2,421 and 4,475 m, evaluated under a protocol in which every model,
  hyperparameter and the primary system were frozen before two blind years
  (July 2022 to June 2024) were scored. The system combines quantile forecasts
  from ridge regression, gradient boosting, a long short-term memory network
  and the Chronos time-series foundation model, trained on leakage-free
  anomalies with local and large-scale (El Niño–Southern Oscillation,
  Madden–Julian Oscillation) predictors, and is compared with the
  bias-corrected Climate Forecast System version 2 (CFSv2). The ensemble
  improves on climatology at every horizon (continuous ranked probability
  skill score 0.30, 0.30 and 0.35 at weeks 1, 2 and 3–4), but its 90%
  intervals cover only 0.63–0.75 of the outcomes; a conformal calibration
  selected on development years brings the coverage to 0.87–0.90. A ridge
  model that uses the CFSv2 forecast as a predictor reaches skill scores of
  0.42, 0.38 and 0.41: it matches CFSv2 at week 1 and improves on it at weeks
  2 and 3–4. Unadapted Chronos is over-confident (coverage 0.22–0.31) until it
  receives absolute-temperature context. These results, partly from analyses
  declared after the blind scores were seen, indicate that calibrated
  subseasonal guidance is attainable at high-elevation stations when
  statistical learning and dynamical forecasts are combined.

# Introduction

Air temperature in the high Andes changes over a few kilometres of distance
and a few hundred metres of elevation, and its week-to-week anomalies decide
whether a frost damages a potato crop, whether pastures recover after a cold
spell, or whether irrigation can be postponed [@Condori2014; @LopezMoreno2015; @Pepin2015].
Forecasts between two and four weeks ahead fall in the subseasonal range,
which has long been called a predictability gap: too far for the atmospheric
initial conditions to dominate and too close for the slowly varying boundary
conditions that drive seasonal forecasts [@Vitart2017; @Robertson2015;
@Mariotti2018]. Operational subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) systems have
narrowed that gap over the last decade, and their skill is known to depend on
windows of opportunity such as the state of the El Niño–Southern Oscillation
(ENSO) and the Madden–Julian Oscillation (MJO) [@Mariotti2020; @Domeisen2022;
@White2022]. Their grid cells, however, do not resolve the stations at which
decisions are taken, and their raw output needs statistical correction before
it is useful at a point [@Monhart2018; @Robertson2023].

Machine learning has become a natural candidate for that correction and, more
ambitiously, for forecasting the anomalies directly. Gradient-boosted trees,
regularised linear models and neural networks have been benchmarked against
dynamical models for subseasonal temperature over the contiguous United
States [@Hwang2019; @He2021; @Mouatadid2023usa] and globally [@Weyn2021;
@Chen2024], and probabilistic neural post-processing improves ensemble
forecasts [@RaspLerch2018; @Scheuerer2020]. Three aspects of this
literature limit what it says about high-mountain stations. First, most
evaluations use reanalysis grids in the mid-latitudes, where ENSO and the MJO
act differently from the tropical Andes [@Garreaud2009; @Sulca2018]. Second,
few studies freeze the model choice before scoring a blind period, although
temporal cross-validation without such a separation can overstate skill
[@Tashman2000; @Bergmeir2012; @Roberts2017]. Third, time-series foundation
models such as Chronos [@Ansari2024] are now offered as zero-shot
forecasters, but how their predictive distributions behave on a physical
target with strong seasonality has not been examined in this setting; nor has
the value of combining station-based learning with an operational dynamical
forecast been quantified for the Andes.

This paper addresses these points with a forecasting system for weekly mean
temperature anomalies at five Peruvian stations between 2,421 and 4,475 m and
an evaluation designed to be hard to over-interpret. Its contributions are:

- **A blind evaluation protocol for subseasonal machine learning.** All
  models, hyperparameters and the primary ensemble were fixed on three
  development years and frozen before two blind years were scored; every
  later analysis is declared as a dated amendment, and every comparison is
  tested with a moving-block bootstrap and Holm's correction.
- **A hybrid dynamical–statistical model.** A ridge regression that uses the
  bias-corrected forecast of the Climate Forecast System version 2 (CFSv2)
  as one more predictor, evaluated against a control fitted on exactly the
  same rows without that predictor, so that its gain can be attributed.
- **A diagnosis of a time-series foundation model on a physical target.** We
  show why Chronos produces intervals that are too narrow for window-mean
  anomalies and how an absolute-temperature context, or the Chronos-Bolt
  variant, changes the balance between calibration and sharpness.
- **Calibrated probabilistic forecasts.** A conformal calibration of the
  ensemble, selected on development years only, which corrects the
  over-confidence of the combined forecast.

Section @sec-related reviews the related work. Section @sec-data describes the stations and
predictors, Section @sec-methods the forecasting system and its evaluation, and
Section @sec-results the blind results. Section @sec-discussion discusses them against the
literature and states the limitations, and Section @sec-conclusions concludes.

# Related work {#sec-related}

## Subseasonal prediction and windows of opportunity

The S2S prediction project established a common framework of weekly and
fortnightly targets, reforecasts and verification for the one-to-eight-week
range [@Vitart2017; @VitartRobertson2018]. Skill at these leads is
intermittent: it depends on whether the initial state contains a slowly
evolving signal, such as an active MJO, a developing ENSO event or
persistent soil-moisture anomalies [@Mariotti2018; @Mariotti2020;
@Domeisen2022]. The MJO modulates tropical convection and, through it,
temperature and rainfall far from its centre of action
[@WheelerHendon2004; @Kiladis2014], and the reforecasts of the Subseasonal
Experiment showed how strongly verification depends on these states
[@Pegion2019]. The practical response has been to report skill
conditioned on the state at issuance, a practice we follow.

## Machine learning for subseasonal temperature

Statistical baselines remain strong at these leads: damped persistence and
climatology are hard to beat beyond two weeks [@Hwang2019; @DelSoleTippett2014],
which is why both are used as references throughout. Gradient-boosted trees
[@Ke2017] and regularised regressions on large-scale indices compete with
dynamical models for weeks 3–4 over North America [@He2021;
@Mouatadid2023usa], and deep architectures such as recurrent networks
[@Hochreiter1997], temporal fusion transformers [@Lim2021] or global
convolutional models [@Weyn2021; @Chen2024] extend the approach. For
hydrological forecasting at many gauges, a single recurrent network trained on
all basins transfers to ungauged ones [@Kratzert2019hess; @Kratzert2019wrr], a
result that motivates our leave-one-station-out test. Reviews of the field
note that gains over simple models are often smaller than architectural
complexity suggests [@Petropoulos2022; @Slater2023].

## Time-series foundation models

Foundation models pretrained on large collections of time series now produce
probabilistic forecasts without task-specific training. Chronos tokenises
scaled values and samples future trajectories from a language-model
architecture [@Ansari2024]; related work explores foundation models and
large language models for forecasting more broadly [@Liang2024; @Tan2024].
Their benchmarks emphasise short-horizon accuracy on heterogeneous datasets;
the calibration of window-averaged quantities derived from their sample paths,
which is what a subseasonal user needs, has received little attention.

## Post-processing and hybrids with dynamical models

Raw dynamical forecasts at subseasonal leads are biased and under-dispersive
at stations, and simple local corrections recover much of their value
[@Monhart2018]. CFSv2 is a widely used coupled system whose reforecasts are
openly available [@Saha2014]. Statistical post-processing ranges from
regression on the ensemble mean to ensemble model output statistics (EMOS)
[@Gneiting2005] and neural networks [@RaspLerch2018]; machine-learning models
that take dynamical forecasts as inputs or correct their biases have improved
subseasonal temperature over North America [@He2021; @Mouatadid2023abc], and
hybrid forecasting that blends climate predictions with machine learning is an
active field [@Slater2023]. Whether such a hybrid adds value over both of its
components at tropical mountain stations is one of the questions addressed
here.

## Probabilistic verification and calibration

A probabilistic forecast should be as sharp as possible subject to being
calibrated [@Gneiting2007]. The continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) is
the standard proper score for continuous variables [@Hersbach2000;
@GneitingRaftery2007], and the probability integral transform (PIT) and
interval coverage diagnose calibration [@Hamill2001; @GneitingRanjan2011].
Combining forecasts by averaging their quantiles (Vincentization) tends to
produce sharper but possibly over-confident distributions, whereas linear
pooling widens them [@Genest1992; @Lichtendahl2013]. Conformal prediction
offers finite-sample coverage guarantees for any model and has been extended
to quantile regression [@Romano2019; @AngelopoulosBates2023]; we use it as one
of the candidate calibrations of the ensemble.

## Temperature variability in the tropical Andes

Interannual temperature variability in the tropical Andes is dominated by
ENSO, with warm anomalies during El Niño and a modulation by the regional
coastal and central-Pacific modes [@Vuille2000; @VuilleBradley2000;
@Garreaud2009]. The coastal (Niño 1+2) and central-Pacific (Niño 3.4) sectors
affect Peru differently, which led to the E and C indices
[@Takahashi2011]; ENSO teleconnections to Andean temperature and rainfall
have been documented for the Altiplano and the western slope
[@LavadoEspinoza2014; @Sulca2018; @Imfeld2020]. Warming is
elevation-dependent [@Pepin2015], and the observing network is sparse and
heterogeneous, which makes quality control an integral part of any
station-based study [@Hunziker2017; @Condori2014].

# Study area and data {#sec-data}

## Stations

We use hourly records from five automatic stations of the Peruvian national
meteorological service, SENAMHI, published as an open dataset [@SENAMHI2024]
whose variables are defined in the provider's data dictionary
[@SENAMHI2024dict], selected to span the western
Andean slope and the Altiplano margin from 2,421 to 4,475 m
(Fig. @fig-study; Table @tbl-stations). Two belong to the global basic observing network
(GBON) and three to the regional one (RBON). The common record runs from
1 January 2015 to 30 June 2024 (3,469 days per station). The harmonic
climatologies in Fig. @fig-study b illustrate the gradient: the mean daily
temperature drops by about 12 °C from Matucana to Imata, and the amplitude of
the annual cycle at the highest station is about three times that at the
lowest.

## Quality control and daily aggregation

The hourly file contains 416,273 station-hours. We first verified the time
convention (the diurnal cycle peaks at 13:00 and bottoms at 06:00 local time,
consistent with local civil time), the 24-hour coverage and the absence of
duplicated timestamps, and treated empty fields as missing; 13,268
station-hours (3.2%) have no variable at all. Temperature values then went
through range, spike and stuck-sensor checks adapted from
@Hunziker2017: 428 spikes and 2,114 stuck-sensor hours were flagged. Daily
means were computed from the remaining hours, and a day was kept only when
enough hours were valid; targets were never imputed.

## Large-scale indices and the dynamical forecast {#sec-largescale}

The large-scale predictors are the weekly Niño 3.4 and Niño 1+2 sea-surface
temperature anomalies from the NOAA optimum interpolation analysis
[@Reynolds2002; @NOAACPCWeeklySST], used with a seven-day publication lag,
and the two components and amplitude of the real-time outgoing-longwave-
radiation MJO index (ROMI) [@Kiladis2014; @Wang2018; @NOAAPSLROMI], used with
a one-day lag. The E and C indices [@Takahashi2011; @IGPECIndex] enter only
as a sensitivity analysis. Indices published with a delay longer than the
issuance (such as the Oceanic Niño Index) were excluded to avoid look-ahead.
The dynamical forecast is the four-member 00 UTC CFSv2 run issued each Monday
[@Saha2014; @NOAACFSv2Open], whose 6-hourly 2 m temperature on the 1° grid was
interpolated bilinearly to each station and averaged over each target window; the open archive starts on
31 October 2018.

# Methodology {#sec-methods}

## Problem formulation

A forecast is issued every Monday $t$ for each station $s$ and three targets:
the mean temperature anomaly over days 1–7 (week 1, W1), days 8–14 (week 2,
W2) and days 15–28 (weeks 3–4, W3–4) after issuance. Window means are the
standard S2S target because day-to-day weather is unpredictable at these
leads while averages retain signal [@Vitart2017; @Robertson2015;
@Pegion2019], and the same three windows are used by recent machine-learning
benchmarks [@Hwang2019; @He2021; @Mouatadid2023usa]. Each horizon has its own
model (direct strategy), so no forecast is fed back as an input. Models are
trained on issuances made every day of the training period, which multiplies
the sample size, and evaluated on Mondays only. The complete system is shown
in Fig. @fig-workflow.

![Forecasting system, from station data to blind evaluation.](media/Fig02_workflow.pdf){#fig-workflow width=1}

## Anomaly decomposition

All models forecast anomalies with respect to a climatology fitted only on
each fold's training days, so that no information from the test period enters
the reference. The climatology of station $s$ is a harmonic regression of the
daily mean temperature on the day of the year $d$
[@Epstein1991], Eq. @eq-clim:

$$
c_s(d) = a_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{K} \left[ a_k \cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi k d}{P}\right) + b_k \sin\!\left(\frac{2\pi k d}{P}\right) \right], \qquad K = 3,\; P = 365.25,
$$ {#eq-clim}

with $K = 3$ chosen on the development years against $K = 1$ and $K = 5$
by the out-of-sample variance of the monthly mean residual. Three harmonics
capture the asymmetric annual cycle of the Altiplano stations, which a single
harmonic cannot represent [@VuilleBradley2000; @Pepin2015]. The target (Eq. @eq-target) is the
mean anomaly over the window $\mathcal{W}_h$ of horizon $h$,

$$
y_{s,t,h} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{W}_h|} \sum_{\ell \in \mathcal{W}_h} \left[ T_s(t+\ell) - c_s\big(d(t+\ell)\big) \right],
$$ {#eq-target}

where $T_s$ is the daily mean temperature. A window counts only when at least
5 of 7 (W1, W2) or 10 of 14 (W3–4) days are valid.

## Predictors

The local predictor set (L) contains lagged daily temperature anomalies (lags
0–6 days) and their 7-, 14- and 30-day means, anomalies of the diurnal
temperature range, daily maximum and minimum temperature and relative
humidity, log-transformed 7- and 30-day rainfall totals, and the sine and
cosine of the target day of the year, all computed from trailing windows that
end on the issuance date; persistence of recent anomalies is the main source of skill
at week 1 [@DelSoleTippett2014]. The large-scale set (G) adds the Niño 3.4,
Niño 1+2 and ROMI predictors described above, because ENSO and the MJO are the
main sources of subseasonal predictability for the region
[@LavadoEspinoza2014; @Sulca2018; @Mariotti2020]. Models with the suffix LG
use L and G, models with the suffix L only L, which isolates the
contribution of the large-scale indices. The CFSv2 predictor is described in
Section @sec-hybrid. Table @tbl-models summarises inputs and outputs.

## Forecasting models

**References.** Climatology and damped persistence are the references against
which skill is measured, because a subseasonal forecast is only useful if it
improves on what these simple rules already provide [@Murphy1993;
@DelSoleTippett2014]. Damped persistence regresses the target on the most
recent 7-day anomaly $A^{(7)}_{s,t}$ for each station, horizon and season
quarter $q$ (Eq. @eq-damp):

$$
\hat{y}_{s,t,h} = \beta_{0,shq} + \beta_{1,shq}\, A^{(7)}_{s,t}, \qquad Y \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(\hat{y}, \sigma^2_{shq}\right),
$$ {#eq-damp}

with $\sigma_{shq}$ the standard deviation of the training residuals of that
cell. The bias-corrected CFSv2 forecast (CFS_BC) follows the station-level
correction of @Monhart2018: the CFSv2 window mean $F_{s,t,h}$ is converted to
an anomaly with respect to its own harmonic climatology $\tilde{c}_{sh}$
($K = 2$, fitted on the training Mondays), and the observed anomaly is
regressed on it,

$$
f_{s,t,h} = F_{s,t,h} - \tilde{c}_{sh}\big(d_{\mathrm{mid}}\big), \qquad \hat{y}_{s,t,h} = \gamma_{0,sh} + \gamma_{1,sh}\, f_{s,t,h},
$$ {#eq-cfs}

with a Gaussian distribution whose standard deviation is that of the training
residuals by quarter, as for damped persistence, so that differences in CRPS
come from the mean.

**Ridge regression.** A standardised ridge regression per station and
horizon, with the penalty chosen on the last training year separated by the
embargo, is the simplest learned model; its predictive distribution is
Gaussian with the inner-validation residual standard deviation by quarter.

**Gradient boosting.** LightGBM [@Ke2017] is pooled over stations per horizon,
with elevation, latitude and longitude as static descriptors. One model is
fitted per quantile level $\tau$ by minimising the pinball loss of quantile
regression [@KoenkerBassett1978] (Eq. @eq-pinball),

$$
\rho_\tau(u) = u\,\big(\tau - \mathbb{1}\{u < 0\}\big), \qquad \hat{q}_\tau = \arg\min_{q} \sum_i \rho_\tau\big(y_i - q(x_i)\big),
$$ {#eq-pinball}

and quantile crossings are removed by rearrangement, which never increases
the quantile loss [@Chernozhukov2010].

**Long short-term memory network.** An LSTM [@Hochreiter1997] reads 60-day
sequences of the LG predictors, together with the static descriptors of the
station, and is trained on all stations at once, following the regional
training strategy of @Kratzert2019hess; it outputs the 19 quantiles with the
pinball loss, with early stopping on the last training dates separated by the
embargo.

**Time-series foundation model.** Chronos-T5-small [@Ansari2024] forecasts
the daily anomaly series from a 512-day context, and each of its 100 sample
paths is averaged over the target window, which gives an empirical
distribution of the window mean. After the first blind scores showed
intervals that were far too narrow (Section @sec-chronos), amendment A3 added two
configurations: Chronos with the absolute temperature as context, the
climatology being subtracted afterwards, and Chronos-Bolt, which returns
quantiles of weekly and fortnightly block means directly. All Chronos
variants are used zero-shot, without fine-tuning. Table @tbl-hyper lists every
hyperparameter.

## Ensemble and calibration

The primary system M\* averages the quantiles of the candidate models
(Vincentization) with weights inversely proportional to their mean CRPS on
the development folds, per horizon (Eq. @eq-vincent):

$$
q^{\mathrm{M}^*}_{\tau} = \sum_{m} w_{m,h}\, q^{(m)}_{\tau}, \qquad w_{m,h} = \frac{1/\overline{\mathrm{CRPS}}^{\,\mathrm{dev}}_{m,h}}{\sum_{m'} 1/\overline{\mathrm{CRPS}}^{\,\mathrm{dev}}_{m',h}}.
$$ {#eq-vincent}

Combining forecasts generally reduces error relative to the members
[@BatesGranger1969; @Busetti2017], and Vincentization keeps the combined
distribution sharp [@Genest1992; @Lichtendahl2013]. M\* was chosen as primary
because its pooled development CRPS (0.3926 °C) was the lowest among the
candidates, ahead of Ridge LG (0.3943 °C), LSTM LG (0.3946 °C) and GBM LG
(0.4207 °C); the weights were close to equal (0.22–0.27 per member).

Vincentization is known to produce over-confident distributions when the
members disagree [@Lichtendahl2013], and the blind coverage of M\* confirmed
this (Section @sec-calibration). Amendment A3 therefore defined M\*~2~, chosen on the
development folds only among 16 configurations: two member sets (with or
without the best Chronos variant), two combinations (Vincentization or linear
pool) and four calibrations per horizon (none, a spread factor, EMOS
[@Gneiting2005] and conformalised quantiles [@Romano2019;
@AngelopoulosBates2023]). The conformal calibration widens each central pair
of quantiles $(\tau, 1-\tau)$ by the empirical quantile of the conformity
score on the calibration rows (Eq. @eq-conformal),

$$
E_i = \max\!\left(q_{\tau,i} - y_i,\; y_i - q_{1-\tau,i}\right), \qquad \delta_\tau = \hat{Q}_{\lceil (n+1)(1-2\tau) \rceil / n}\big(\{E_i\}\big), \qquad \tilde{q}_\tau = q_\tau - \delta_\tau,\; \tilde{q}_{1-\tau} = q_{1-\tau} + \delta_\tau ,
$$ {#eq-conformal}

leaving the median unchanged. Weights and calibrations were cross-fitted
(fitted on two development folds, scored on the third), and the winner was
the configuration with the lowest cross-fitted CRPS whose 90% coverage lay in
0.85–0.95 at every horizon. It was refitted on all development years and
written to disk before any blind row was scored.

## Hybrid dynamical–statistical model {#sec-hybrid}

Amendment A5, written after the blind scores of M\* and CFS_BC were known,
tests whether the two sources of information are complementary. The hybrid
(Eq. @eq-hybrid) adds the CFSv2 anomaly of Eq. @eq-cfs to the ridge regression of Ridge LG,

$$
\hat{\mu}_{s,t,h} = \beta_0 + \boldsymbol{\beta}_L^{\top} \mathbf{x}^{L}_{s,t} + \boldsymbol{\beta}_G^{\top} \mathbf{x}^{G}_{t} + \beta_F\, f_{s,t,h}, \qquad \min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \sum_i \left(y_i - \hat{\mu}_i\right)^2 + \lambda \lVert \boldsymbol{\beta}_{-0} \rVert_2^2 ,
$$ {#eq-hybrid}

with the same penalty grid, inner validation and residual distribution as
Ridge LG. Using a dynamical forecast as a predictor of a statistical model
follows earlier subseasonal hybrids [@He2021; @Mouatadid2023abc]. Because the
CFSv2 archive starts in October 2018, the hybrid can only be trained in the
blind folds, on about 185 training Mondays per station and horizon, and
nothing could be tuned. To separate the effect of the CFSv2 predictor from
that of the shorter, weekly training sample, we fitted a control with the
same rows and without $f$; this control has no direct precedent in the
literature and follows from the logic of a paired ablation. We also report a
gradient-boosting hybrid and an untrained blend, the equal-weight quantile
average of CFS_BC and M\*.

## Validation design and leakage control

Figure @fig-design shows the design. Five one-year test folds, from July to June,
are evaluated with an expanding training window that starts on 1 January
2015 (rolling origin; @Tashman2000). The first three folds (D1–D3,
2019–2022) were used for development; the last two (B1, B2, July 2022 to
June 2024) were blind. A 28-day embargo separates the last training target
from the first test day, so that no training window overlaps a test window,
as required for serially dependent data [@Bergmeir2012; @Roberts2017]. The
climatology, scalers, penalties, residual distributions and ensemble weights
are all estimated on training rows only. Hyperparameters and the primary
model were frozen before B1; the blind folds contain 102, 100 and 96
issuance dates at W1, W2 and W3–4 (506, 497 and 478 station forecasts).
Because a W3–4 forecast issued in June would have a target in the next fold's
test year, those issuances are not evaluated in either fold. Transfer to
stations without history was tested by leave-one-station-out (LOSO) training
of the pooled models on the blind folds [@Kratzert2019wrr]. In Fig. @fig-design, El Niño and La Niña episodes are periods of at least 60 days in which the 91-day mean Niño 3.4 anomaly exceeds +0.5 °C or falls below $-0.5$ °C.

![Validation design: expanding training windows, 28-day embargo, development and blind test years, CFSv2 archive and ENSO episodes; models were frozen at the dashed line.](media/Fig03_validation_design.pdf){#fig-design width=1}

**Reproducibility.** The pipeline, its configuration and the two notebooks
that run it end to end are archived on Zenodo [@c20-2026-code], and the station
data are the open dataset described in Section @sec-data [@SENAMHI2024]. Every
number in this paper is read from a machine-readable output of that pipeline.

## Verification metrics

The CRPS is computed from the 19 quantiles as twice the mean pinball loss,
which approximates the integral of the quantile score over $\tau$
[@GneitingRaftery2007; @Hersbach2000] (Eq. @eq-crps):

$$
\mathrm{CRPS}(F, y) \approx \frac{2}{|\mathcal{T}|} \sum_{\tau \in \mathcal{T}} \rho_\tau\big(y - q_\tau\big).
$$ {#eq-crps}

Skill against a reference $r$ is reported as a skill score computed from the
sums over all stations and issuances, which weights each forecast equally and
avoids the instability of averaging per-case ratios [@Murphy1988; @Wilks2019] (Eq. @eq-skill):

$$
\mathrm{CRPSS}_r = 1 - \frac{\sum_{i} \mathrm{CRPS}_{i}}{\sum_{i} \mathrm{CRPS}^{(r)}_{i}}, \qquad \mathrm{MSSS}_r = 1 - \frac{\sum_{i} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{\sum_{i} (y_i - \hat{y}^{(r)}_i)^2}.
$$ {#eq-skill}

Calibration is diagnosed with the 90% interval coverage and the PIT
[@Hamill2001; @GneitingRanjan2011] (Eq. @eq-coverage):

$$
\mathrm{Cov}_{90} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbb{1}\{q_{0.05,i} \le y_i \le q_{0.95,i}\}, \qquad u_i = \hat{F}_i(y_i),
$$ {#eq-coverage}

where a calibrated forecast has $\mathrm{Cov}_{90} \approx 0.90$ and uniform
PIT values; coverage in 0.85–0.95 was the pre-registered criterion. We also
report the mean absolute error, root-mean-square error, anomaly correlation
(ACC), the ranked probability skill score for terciles (RPSS) [@Epstein1969]
and the mean width of the 90% interval as a measure of sharpness.

## Statistical inference and pre-registration

All tests use the blind folds only, with stations pooled. Because the
forecasts of consecutive weeks and of different stations are correlated,
differences are aggregated per issuance date and resampled by a moving-block
bootstrap of 8 weeks [@Kunsch1989], with the same blocks for every station;
the nested ridge comparison uses the Clark–West statistic with a
heteroscedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent variance
[@ClarkWest2007; @NeweyWest1987]. A one-sided p-value is the share of
bootstrap replicates of the centred statistic at least as large as the
observed one, and p-values are adjusted by Holm's procedure within each
family of three horizons [@Holm1979; @Wilks2016] (Eq. @eq-test):

$$
p = \frac{1 + \#\{b : \Delta^*_b - \bar{\Delta} \ge \bar{\Delta}\}}{B + 1}, \qquad p^{\mathrm{Holm}}_{(j)} = \max_{i \le j} \min\!\big(1, (m - i + 1)\, p_{(i)}\big).
$$ {#eq-test}

The design, the hypotheses H1–H4 and the decision rule were written before
any score existed; analyses added after the blind scores were seen are dated
amendments, reported as such (Table @tbl-hypotheses).

# Results {#sec-results}

## Blind skill overview

Figure @fig-skill and Tables [-@tbl-metrics]–[-@tbl-metrics-w34] summarise the blind results. Every learned model
improves on climatology at every horizon, and every one except raw Chronos
improves on damped persistence. Two patterns stand out. CFS_BC is the best
single system at W1 (CRPSS against climatology 0.415, 95% interval
0.32–0.50), but its skill falls to 0.218 (0.14–0.28) at W3–4, the steepest
decline of any system; the dynamical forecast is most useful where its
initial conditions still matter, as expected from the S2S literature
[@Vitart2017; @Pegion2019]. The statistical and machine-learning models
follow the opposite course: their skill is flat or increases with the
horizon, from 0.297 to 0.385 for Ridge LG and from 0.273 to 0.378 for LSTM
LG. Window means over 14 days filter out unpredictable daily weather and keep
the slowly varying component driven by persistence and large-scale indices,
the mechanism that @Mariotti2018 and @Domeisen2022 identify as the source of
subseasonal skill.

![Blind skill by horizon against (a) climatology and (b) damped persistence, with 95% intervals; filled markers: interval above zero.](media/Fig04_blind_skill.pdf){#fig-skill width=1}

The primary ensemble M\* has CRPSS of 0.295 (0.20–0.39), 0.298 (0.20–0.38)
and 0.345 (0.24–0.43) against climatology, which supports H3 (Holm
p = 0.0003 at each horizon), and its mean-square skill against damped
persistence at W3–4 is 0.409 (one-sided 95% lower bound 0.339; p = 0.0001),
which supports H2. M\* is not, however, better than its best member: Ridge LG
reaches 0.297, 0.324 and 0.385, within the sampling uncertainty of M\* at
every horizon. The deterministic metrics tell the same story (Table @tbl-metrics-w34).
At W3–4 Ridge LG has the lowest root-mean-square error (0.612 °C) and the
highest mean-square skill (0.598), and LSTM LG has the highest anomaly
correlation together with M\* (0.794 and 0.795).

## Value of the large-scale predictors

The comparison of each model with and without the ENSO and MJO predictors
tests H1 (Table @tbl-tests; Fig. @fig-budget). For the ridge regression the gain is
clear at every horizon: the Clark–West statistics are 4.10, 4.56 and 4.55
(Holm p < $10^{-4}$), and the CRPS difference is 0.22, 0.34 and 0.41 °C summed
over stations per issuance (Holm p = 0.016, 0.009 and 0.009). For gradient
boosting the large-scale predictors help at W2 and W3–4 (Holm p = 0.048 and
0.004 for CRPS) but not at W1 (p = 0.26). The pattern, no gain from remote
indices at week 1 and an increasing gain after it, agrees with the
windows-of-opportunity view in which persistence dominates the first week and
slowly varying modes the following ones [@Mariotti2020; @Domeisen2022].
Replacing the Niño indices by the E and C indices of @Takahashi2011 changes
the CRPSS of Ridge LG and GBM LG by at most 0.02 (sensitivity runs, not
tabulated), so the result does not depend on how ENSO is described.

## Against the dynamical model and the hybrid

The pre-registered comparison with CFS_BC (H4) is mixed. M\* is clearly
worse at W1 ($\Delta$CRPS $-0.419$), indistinguishable at W2 (0.001; Holm p = 0.69)
and better at W3–4 (0.383; Holm p = 0.012). The crossover between a
dynamical forecast that is strong early and a statistical one that is
stronger later reproduces, at stations and at a tropical latitude, what
@Monhart2018 found for bias-corrected European forecasts and @He2021 and
@Mouatadid2023usa found for North America.

The hybrid of amendment A5 exploits that crossover (Fig. @fig-hybrid; Table @tbl-ci). It
reaches CRPSS of 0.424 (0.34–0.50), 0.384 (0.26–0.50) and 0.411 (0.28–0.53),
the highest point estimates of any system at W1 and W2 and the second highest
at W3–4. Against CFS_BC it is indistinguishable at W1 ($\Delta$CRPS 0.031;
p = 0.26) and better at W2 and W3–4 (Holm p = 0.012 and 0.002); against M\*
it is better at all three horizons (Holm p = 0.0003, 0.017 and 0.031). The
same-rows control shows that the gain comes from the CFSv2 predictor rather
than from the weekly training sample: the hybrid beats it by 0.462 and 0.262
at W1 and W2 (Holm p = 0.0003 and 0.012), and by a small margin at W3–4
(0.035; Holm p = 0.026, two-sided interval $-0.006$ to 0.070), where the
CFSv2 signal itself is weak. The correlation between the bias-corrected
CFSv2 anomaly and the observation falls from 0.70 at W1 to 0.21 at W3–4 on
the blind folds, which explains why the hybrid converges towards its control
at the longest horizon. These results are post hoc and the hybrid was not
tuned; they suggest, rather than establish, that a regularised linear
combination of station predictors and a dynamical forecast is the most
skilful of the systems tested.

![Paired CRPS differences of the hybrid and the blend against their references, with 95% intervals; filled markers: Holm-adjusted p < 0.05.](media/Fig05_hybrid_tests.pdf){#fig-hybrid width=0.55}

Two other hybrids behave differently. The gradient-boosting hybrid also
improves on its own control at every horizon (Holm p $\le 0.004$), but with
about 185 Mondays per station its quantile models are poorly calibrated (90%
coverage 0.47–0.70) and it does not beat CFS_BC. The untrained blend matches
CFS_BC at W1 and improves on it at W3–4 (Holm p = 0.001), but it is worse
than M\* at W3–4, because equal weights give the weak CFSv2 forecast too much
influence at that lead. A regularised model that learns how much to trust
the dynamical forecast at each horizon is therefore preferable to a fixed
combination, consistent with the post-processing literature
[@RaspLerch2018; @Slater2023].

## Calibration of the ensemble {#sec-calibration}

M\* is skilful but over-confident (Fig. @fig-calibration). Its blind 90% interval
covers 0.753, 0.686 and 0.630 of the outcomes, outside the pre-registered
0.85–0.95, and its PIT histogram at W3–4 is U-shaped, with 17% and 32% of the
outcomes in the lowest and highest deciles. The cause is the Vincentization
of members that disagree [@Lichtendahl2013]: averaging quantiles narrows the
distribution exactly when member uncertainty is largest. The dev-selected
M\*~2~ combines the same members with Chronos (absolute context) and a
conformal calibration. Its coverage is 0.903, 0.887 and 0.866, within the
target range, and its CRPS is lower than that of M\* at all horizons (H5;
Holm p $\le 0.002$), with CRPSS of 0.323, 0.348 and 0.426. The selection is
visible in Table @tbl-mstar2 (Section @sec-app-tables): the conformal calibration had the lowest
cross-fitted development CRPS among the in-range configurations, and EMOS,
although best on the blind CRPS (0.398 °C against 0.415 °C), was not chosen
because its development coverage at W3–4 (0.872) was in range but its
development CRPS was higher (0.395 °C against 0.382 °C). Reporting all
candidates keeps the post hoc selection auditable. The hybrid, which has no
calibration step, covers 0.81–0.84; CFS_BC covers 0.85 at W1 but only 0.73 at
W3–4.

![Calibration on the blind folds: (a) 90% interval coverage, with the nominal band; (b) PIT histograms at weeks 3–4.](media/Fig06_calibration.pdf){#fig-calibration width=1}

## Adapting the time-series foundation model {#sec-chronos}

Raw Chronos, used zero-shot on the daily anomaly series, has the lowest
probabilistic skill of the learned models (CRPSS 0.126, 0.087 and 0.105)
despite an anomaly correlation (0.64–0.69) similar to that of the other
models (Fig. @fig-chronos; Tables [-@tbl-metrics]–[-@tbl-metrics-w34]). Its intervals are the problem: they
cover 0.22–0.31 of the outcomes and are 0.5–0.6 °C wide, less than half the
width of any other system. The diagnostic of amendment A2 locates the
cause in the daily paths. Their 90% interval covers 0.21–0.22 of the daily
anomalies, and their spread is about one fifth of the error of their median
(path standard deviation 0.20–0.24 °C against 1.14–1.32 °C), so averaging
them over a window cannot recover the missing spread. With absolute
temperature as context, the model sees the seasonal cycle it was pretrained
on, and its window-mean intervals widen to 2.0–2.4 °C with coverage
0.74–0.86 and CRPSS 0.271, 0.256 and 0.320, comparable to GBM LG.
Chronos-Bolt, which forecasts block means directly, reaches nominal coverage
(0.90–0.95) but with intervals of 3.1–3.5 °C, the widest of any system, and
its CRPSS (0.18–0.22) stays below that of Chronos with absolute context. The
three variants span the balance between calibration and sharpness that
@Gneiting2007 describe: a forecast can be calibrated by being vague, and a
proper score rewards the system that is sharp subject to calibration.

![Chronos variants on the blind folds: (a) skill, (b) 90% interval coverage and (c) interval width, with M\* as reference.](media/Fig07_chronos.pdf){#fig-chronos width=1}

## Robustness

**Windows of opportunity.** Skill depends on the state of ENSO at issuance
(Fig. @fig-conditional). The CRPSS of M\* is 0.37–0.43 when El Niño conditions
prevail (n = 240–250 forecasts), 0.16–0.23 under La Niña (n = 175) and
0.06–0.20 in neutral conditions (n = 63–81). It is also higher in austral
summer (0.39–0.46 in December–February) than in winter (0.15–0.31 in
June–August), and slightly higher with an active MJO (0.32–0.38) than with
an inactive one (0.26–0.32). Skill is positive in every condition, so it is
not confined to the 2023–24 El Niño, but that event contributes a large
share of the blind forecasts; this dependence on the regime is what
@Mariotti2020 call a window of opportunity, and it matches the strong ENSO
control of Andean temperature [@Vuille2000; @Garreaud2009]. These splits are
descriptive, and the neutral cell is small.

![Skill of M\* by (a) ENSO phase, (b) season and (c) MJO activity at issuance (blind folds).](media/Fig08_conditional_skill.pdf){#fig-conditional width=1}

**Transfer to unseen stations.** When the pooled models are trained without
the station they forecast, their skill changes little (Fig. @fig-loso). For M\*
the CRPS increases by at most 0.052 °C, and at the two highest stations it
does not increase at all; the largest losses are at San José de Uzuña and
Matucana at W3–4, where the CRPSS drops from 0.41 to 0.34 and from 0.44 to
0.33 (Table @tbl-loso). The pooled models therefore transfer to stations within
the range of the training elevations, as in the multi-basin transfer of
@Kratzert2019wrr, although five stations are too few to test transfer across
climates.

![CRPS lost when a station is left out of training, by station elevation, with 95% intervals.](media/Fig09_loso.pdf){#fig-loso width=1}

**Training noise and period.** Re-training GBM L, GBM LG and LSTM LG with
four additional seeds changes their CRPSS by a standard deviation of at most
0.005 for the gradient-boosting models and 0.020 for the LSTM, and the
ranking GBM L < GBM LG < LSTM LG holds in every seed and horizon
(Table @tbl-seeds; Fig. @fig-seeds in Section @sec-app-figures). All models have higher skill on the blind folds
than on the development folds (Fig. @fig-devblind), M\* for example 0.29–0.35
against 0.12–0.16. The order of the models is preserved, which indicates that
the increase reflects the more predictable blind years, dominated by the
2023–24 El Niño, rather than a model selection effect.

## Case study

Figure @fig-case shows the W3–4 forecasts at San José de Uzuña, the station with the
median hybrid CRPS, chosen before the figure was drawn. During the 2022–23
La Niña the observed anomalies are mostly negative; the hybrid median is
negative too but weaker, and several observations fall near or below the
lower edge of its 90% band. From mid-2023 the anomalies build up with the
onset of El Niño, and the hybrid median follows the rise to about +1.5 °C in
early 2024, above the CFSv2 median, which stays mostly between 0 and +1 °C. M\*~2~ brackets the observations with a
wider band. The gap before July 2023 corresponds to the issuances whose
target would fall in the next fold's test year.

![Weeks 3–4 forecasts at San José de Uzuña (3,269 m) over the blind period; the dotted line marks the B1–B2 fold boundary.](media/Fig10_case_study.pdf){#fig-case width=1}

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

## What the system adds

The central result is that the statistical and dynamical forecasts fail in
different places. CFS_BC is the best single system at W1 and the weakest
among the weakest at W3–4; the station-based models are the reverse. The
hybrid ridge model, which learns how much weight the CFSv2 anomaly deserves
at each horizon, is at least as good as the better of the two at every
horizon. This complementarity has been reported for subseasonal forecasts in
North America [@He2021; @Mouatadid2023abc] and, through bias correction of
dynamical forecasts, for Europe [@Monhart2018], and it is the premise of
hybrid forecasting more broadly [@Slater2023]; our results extend it to
high-elevation stations in the tropics, where ENSO is the dominant source of
predictability [@Vuille2000; @LavadoEspinoza2014; @Sulca2018]. In engineering terms, the hybrid is a
low-cost addition to an existing station-based system: it requires one
dynamical forecast per week and per station and a linear model refitted on a
few hundred cases.

## Lessons for time-series foundation models

Chronos is a capable point forecaster on this problem but, used as offered,
a poor probabilistic one. The problem is not the accuracy of its median but
the spread of its sample paths, which is too small at the daily scale to
survive averaging. Giving the model the absolute temperature, closer to the
data it was pretrained on [@Ansari2024], restores most of the spread, and
Chronos-Bolt shows the opposite failure. For users of foundation models in
environmental applications, the practical implication is that interval
coverage of the derived quantity, not only point accuracy, has to be checked
before such models enter an ensemble, and that the input representation
matters as much as the model choice [@Liang2024; @Tan2024].

## Simple versus complex models

Ridge LG matches or exceeds every more complex model, including the LSTM, the
foundation models and the ensemble, on the blind folds. The gain from adding
the large-scale indices (H1) is larger than any gain from changing the
architecture, and the best gradient-boosting and LSTM models differ by less
than their seed-to-seed range at W1. With about ten years of data at five
stations, the limiting factor is the information in the predictors rather
than the capacity of the model, a conclusion that echoes forecasting
competitions [@Petropoulos2022] and contrasts with settings where large
training sets let deep models learn shared structure across hundreds of
sites [@Kratzert2019hess].

## Operational implications

A forecasting service needs probabilities it can trust. The conformal
calibration selected on development years delivers 90% intervals that cover
close to 90% of the blind outcomes without sacrificing skill, and the case
study shows forecasts that track an evolving El Niño anomaly several weeks in
advance. Both are relevant for frost and agricultural planning, where the
cost of a missed cold anomaly differs from that of a false alarm. The
secondary results support this use: Ridge LG has positive skill for the
minimum temperature at every horizon (CRPSS 0.21–0.28) and for the
probability of frost (Brier skill 0.13–0.29; Table @tbl-secondary), although the
frost index is computed from hourly means and understates true frost.

## Limitations

The study has five limitations that bound its conclusions. (i) Five stations
and two blind years give wide confidence intervals; several differences
between the best systems are not distinguishable, and the results should not
be generalised to the whole Andes without further stations. (ii) The hybrid,
M\*~2~ and the Chronos variants are post hoc; their designs were fixed before
their own scores but after the blind scores of the pre-registered systems,
and they should be confirmed on later years. (iii) The hybrid is trained on
about 185 Mondays per station because the open CFSv2 archive starts in 2018,
and its 90% coverage (0.81–0.84) is below the target range; a calibration
step could not be selected without development years. (iv) The only
dynamical reference is CFSv2 at 1° resolution; the ECMWF extended-range
system, usually the strongest S2S reference, was not available to us, so our
comparison is with an open dynamical forecast rather than with the state of
the art. (v) The blind period includes the 2023–24 El Niño, which raises the
skill of all systems; the conditional results show positive skill in all
ENSO phases, but the size of the gains is tied to that period.

# Conclusions {#sec-conclusions}

Subseasonal temperature forecasts at high-Andean stations can be both skilful
and calibrated, provided that the forecasting system is designed and
evaluated with the same discipline. That is the thread that connects the
methodological and technical results of this study.

On the methodological side, freezing the models and their hyperparameters
before scoring two blind years, separating training and test targets by an
embargo and testing every comparison with a block bootstrap and Holm's
correction made it possible to tell real skill from favourable sampling. The
same protocol exposed what cross-validation alone would have hidden: the
blind years were more predictable than the development years for every
model, and the primary ensemble, although skilful, was over-confident. A
leakage-free anomaly decomposition gave statistical, deep and foundation
models a common target, and declaring every later analysis as a dated
amendment kept the post hoc results distinguishable from the confirmatory
ones, in line with recommendations for forecast evaluation
[@Tashman2000; @Bergmeir2012; @DelSoleTippett2014].

On the technical side, four findings follow. A ridge regression that adds the
bias-corrected CFSv2 forecast to station and large-scale predictors matched
CFSv2 at week 1 and improved on it at weeks 2–4, with skill scores of 0.42,
0.38 and 0.41 against climatology; its same-rows control attributes the gain
to the dynamical predictor, extending to the tropical Andes the
complementarity reported elsewhere [@Monhart2018; @He2021]. The ENSO and MJO
indices contributed more skill than any change of architecture, so that a
regularised linear model was as good as a recurrent network and a foundation
model [@Petropoulos2022]. Chronos, used zero-shot, produced intervals about
four times too narrow for window-mean anomalies until it received
absolute-temperature context, a reminder that foundation models must be
checked for calibration on the quantity a user needs [@Gneiting2007;
@Ansari2024]. Finally, a conformal calibration chosen on development years
turned an over-confident ensemble into one whose 90% intervals covered close
to 90% of the blind outcomes [@Romano2019].

The two sides depend on each other. The technical results are credible
because the protocol was fixed in advance, and the protocol is worth its cost
because the results it validates change what a forecaster can offer for frost
and agricultural decisions. The evidence comes from five stations and two
blind years, and the hybrid and the calibrated ensemble were defined after the
first blind scores; confirming them on later years and more stations, adding
the ECMWF extended-range forecasts and calibrating the hybrid are the next
steps. Within these limits, the study shows that combining station-based
learning with an open dynamical forecast yields calibrated guidance for the
weeks that matter most to Andean farmers and water managers.
